name: ss
one_line: investigate sockets (who is listening, who is connected)
plain: `ss` shows the network connections and listening ports on this machine. It answers: which programs are waiting for connections, and who is connected to whom.
It replaces netstat. The usual call is `ss -tulpn`: TCP, UDP, Listening, Process, Numeric.
when: Check which ports a machine is listening on after you land on it.
See which process owns a port.
Count connections in a given state.

examples.title: Everything that is listening
examples.explain: -t TCP, -u UDP, -l listening only, -p show the process (needs root to see other users' processes), -n numbers not names. This is the most common form.

examples.title: Established connections
examples.explain: Without -l, ss shows connections that exist right now. -n keeps addresses numeric.

examples.title: Who is using port 22?
examples.explain: A filter expression after the options. sport is the local (source) port; dport is the remote port.

examples.title: Connections to a particular host
examples.explain: Only connections whose remote address matches.

examples.title: Count by state
examples.explain: -a includes all states. This counts ESTAB, LISTEN, TIME-WAIT... a quick sense of load.

examples.title: Unix sockets
examples.explain: -x shows Unix domain sockets, which services use to talk locally (docker.sock, mysql.sock).

examples.title: Show timers and memory
examples.explain: -o shows timers, -i shows internal TCP information such as round-trip time.

options.plain: Do not resolve service names or hosts.
Show the process using each socket.
options.use: Finding which program owns a port.

options.plain: Show sockets of this family (inet, inet6, unix, link, netlink).
Dump raw TCP socket data to a file.
Filter by state (established, syn-sent, listening, time-wait...).
Filter by source/destination port or address.

mistakes: Forgetting -n and waiting for slow DNS lookups.
Not using sudo with -p and seeing blanks in the process column.
Reading 0.0.0.0 or [::] as a remote host: it means 'every interface'.
Ignoring 127.0.0.1-only listeners: they are not reachable from outside but can matter after a pivot.
try: Start python3 -m http.server 8000 and find it with ss -tulpn.
List only established connections on port 443.
Compare ss -tlnp with an nmap scan of localhost.
see_also: ip(8), netstat(8), lsof(8), nmap(1), tcpdump(8), fuser(1).
captured_with: Examples are written to explain a technique; they are not captured output.
